title: Feeding a sourdough starter
text: Discard about half of the starter and feed the rest equal weights of flour and water once or twice a day. Regular feeding keeps the yeast and lactic acid bacteria active and stops the culture from becoming too acidic.

title: Storing your starter in the fridge
text: If you bake only on weekends, keep the starter in the refrigerator and feed it once a week. Take it out the day before baking and give it two feedings at room temperature so it is bubbly and doubles in size again.

title: Reviving a neglected starter
text: A grey liquid layer called hooch means the starter is hungry, not dead. Pour it off, discard most of the culture, and feed it fresh flour and water every twelve hours for a few days until it rises predictably.

title: Starter hydration explained
text: Hydration is the ratio of water to flour in a levain. A 100 percent hydration starter is easy to stir and ferments quickly; a stiffer starter ferments more slowly and tolerates longer gaps between feedings.

title: The history of San Francisco sourdough
text: Sourdough became a symbol of San Francisco during the Gold Rush, when miners carried their cultures with them. Bakeries in the city still advertise loaves made from starters that are more than a century old.

title: Yeast strains in home brewing
text: Ale yeast ferments at warmer temperatures and produces fruity esters, while lager yeast works cold and slow. Brewers pitch a healthy starter of yeast into the wort to make sure fermentation begins quickly.

title: Rayleigh scattering
text: Sunlight is scattered by molecules in the atmosphere, and shorter wavelengths scatter far more strongly than longer ones. Blue light is scattered in every direction across the sky, which is why the daytime sky looks blue.

title: Why sunsets are red
text: When the sun is low, its light passes through much more air before reaching you. Most of the blue is scattered out along the way, leaving the reds and oranges that colour sunrise and sunset.

title: Why the sky is not violet
text: Violet light scatters even more than blue, but sunlight contains less violet, some is absorbed high in the atmosphere, and our eyes are less sensitive to it. The combination makes the sky appear blue rather than purple.

title: The colour of the sky on Mars
text: Fine dust suspended in the Martian atmosphere scatters red light, so the daytime sky on Mars looks butterscotch. Sunsets there appear bluish, the reverse of what we see on Earth, because of how the dust particles scatter light.

title: Blue whales
text: The blue whale is the largest animal known to have lived. It feeds almost entirely on krill, filtering tonnes of water through baleen plates every day.

title: The blue screen of death
text: On Windows, a stop error shows a blue screen with an error code when the operating system hits a fault it cannot recover from, often caused by a faulty driver or failing hardware.

title: Finding leaks with tracemalloc
text: Python's built-in tracemalloc module records where memory is allocated. Take a snapshot before and after a suspect operation and compare them to see which lines of code are responsible for the growth.

title: Reference cycles and the garbage collector
text: Objects that refer to each other form cycles that reference counting alone cannot free. The gc module collects them, but cycles involving objects with custom finalizers or caches that keep growing are a common source of memory leaks in long-running Python services.

title: Profiling object growth with objgraph
text: The objgraph package shows which object types are increasing between two points in a program and can draw the chain of references keeping an object alive, which makes it easier to find what is holding on to memory.

title: Unbounded caches in Python
text: A module-level dictionary used as a cache, or an lru_cache with maxsize=None, keeps every entry forever. In a web server this looks like a slow memory leak; bounding the cache size usually fixes it.

title: What pythons eat
text: Pythons are constrictors that feed on rodents, birds and larger mammals. A large python may eat only a few times a year, digesting its prey slowly over several weeks.

title: Choosing a memory foam mattress
text: Memory foam softens with body heat and moulds to your shape, relieving pressure points. Denser foams last longer but can sleep warmer.

title: Iron deficiency anaemia
text: Without enough iron the body cannot make sufficient haemoglobin. Common symptoms include tiredness, shortness of breath on exertion, and a pounding heartbeat.

title: Physical signs of low iron
text: Low iron can cause pale skin, brittle or spoon-shaped nails, hair loss, a sore tongue, and cold hands and feet. Some people also develop cravings to eat ice.

title: Testing ferritin levels
text: Ferritin is the protein that stores iron. A blood test for ferritin is the most useful way to detect low iron stores, often before anaemia develops.

title: Who is at risk of iron deficiency
text: Heavy menstrual periods, pregnancy, frequent blood donation and vegetarian diets low in iron-rich foods all increase the risk of iron deficiency and its symptoms.

title: Seasoning a cast iron skillet
text: Coat a clean cast iron pan with a thin layer of oil and bake it upside down for an hour. Repeat a few times to build a slick, rust-resistant surface.

title: Training for an Ironman triathlon
text: An Ironman combines a 3.8 km swim, a 180 km bike ride and a full marathon. Most training plans build volume gradually over six to nine months.

title: How compound interest works
text: With compound interest you earn interest on the original amount and on the interest already added. Over many years this snowball effect makes balances grow much faster than simple interest would.

title: The compound interest formula
text: The future value of a deposit is P times (1 + r/n) raised to the power n times t, where r is the annual rate, n the number of compounding periods per year, and t the number of years.

title: The rule of 72
text: Divide 72 by the annual interest rate to estimate how many years it takes money to double with compounding. At 6 percent, savings double in roughly twelve years.

title: Why starting to save early matters
text: Because returns compound, money invested in your twenties has decades longer to grow than money invested later, so small early contributions can end up larger than bigger ones made later.

title: Organic compounds
text: An organic compound is a molecule containing carbon bonded to hydrogen. Examples range from methane to proteins and DNA.

title: Credit card interest
text: Credit card interest is usually compounded daily on any unpaid balance, which is why carrying a balance from month to month becomes expensive so quickly.

title: When to plant tomatoes outdoors
text: Plant tomato seedlings outside after the last spring frost, once night temperatures stay above about 10 degrees Celsius and the soil has warmed.

title: Hardening off seedlings
text: Before transplanting, set seedlings outdoors for a few hours a day and lengthen the time over a week or two. This hardening off prevents shock from sun, wind and cooler nights.

title: Starting tomatoes from seed
text: Sow tomato seeds indoors six to eight weeks before your area's last frost date so the plants are a good size when it is warm enough to move them outside.

title: Soil temperature and planting
text: Warm-season crops such as tomatoes and peppers stall in cold soil. A soil thermometer reading of 16 degrees Celsius or more is a reliable sign it is time to plant.

title: Classic tomato sauce
text: Simmer crushed tomatoes with olive oil, garlic and a little salt for about forty minutes, then finish with fresh basil.

title: What causes jet lag
text: Jet lag happens when your internal circadian clock is out of step with the time zone you have flown into, so you feel sleepy or alert at the wrong times.

title: Using light to reset your body clock
text: Bright light is the strongest signal for the circadian clock. After flying east, seek morning light; after flying west, get light in the evening to shift your rhythm faster.

title: Melatonin for jet lag
text: Taking a small dose of melatonin close to the target bedtime at your destination can help the body clock adjust, particularly after eastward flights.

title: Recovering from jet lag
text: Expect to adjust by roughly one time zone per day. Eating meals on local time, staying hydrated, and short naps rather than long ones all help recovery.

title: How jet engines work
text: A turbofan engine sucks in air, compresses it, mixes it with fuel and ignites it. The hot exhaust and the bypass air from the large front fan produce thrust.

title: How vaccines train the immune system
text: A vaccine shows the immune system a harmless piece or version of a pathogen, called an antigen, so it can learn to recognise the real thing without you getting sick.

title: Memory B and T cells
text: After vaccination some B and T cells become long-lived memory cells. If the real pathogen appears later, they respond within days instead of weeks.

title: How mRNA vaccines work
text: mRNA vaccines give cells instructions to make a single viral protein. The immune system responds to that protein and builds antibodies and memory cells against it; the mRNA itself breaks down quickly.

title: Why booster doses are given
text: Antibody levels fall over time after vaccination. A booster re-exposes the immune system to the antigen and strengthens and lengthens its memory response.

title: Antivirus software
text: Antivirus programs scan files for signatures of known malware and watch for suspicious behaviour, quarantining a computer virus before it can spread.

title: The immune system and exercise
text: Moderate regular exercise is associated with fewer colds, while very long intense sessions can temporarily suppress some immune functions.
